lesson.title: Who's Actually Running the Machines
lesson.summary: A miner is the person, company, or coalition that operates the hardware performing proof-of-work mining, motivated not by altruism but by block rewards and transaction fees.
lesson.body:
It is easy to talk about mining as an abstract process, but every hash computed is being run on hardware that someone owns, powers, and pays to maintain. A miner is that someone: an individual, a company, or a pool of participants who dedicate computing equipment to the mining process described earlier, in the hope of earning rewards for their trouble. Understanding miners as economic actors, rather than as anonymous cogs in a security mechanism, is essential to understanding why the system behaves the way it does.

The incentive structure is straightforward but consequential. When a miner successfully finds a valid block, they typically receive two things: a block subsidy of newly created coins, and the transaction fees attached to everything included in that block. The subsidy usually follows a predetermined, shrinking schedule, for example Bitcoin's reward halves roughly every four years, which means the balance between subsidy income and fee income shifts over time. Miners are not securing the network out of civic duty. They are pursuing profit, and the entire security model depends on honest mining being more profitable than attempting to cheat.

Because the odds of any single machine finding a valid block can be extremely low, especially as total network computing power grows, individual miners face large payout variance. A small operation might go months without earning anything on its own, even while contributing real work to the network. This gave rise to mining pools: groups of miners who combine their hashing power, share the search for valid blocks, and split whatever rewards are found in proportion to each participant's contributed effort. Pools smooth out income for individual miners but concentrate influence in the hands of whoever operates the pool's coordination software, which is a real centralization concern even in a supposedly decentralized system.

Miners also respond to costs, particularly electricity and hardware, in ways that shape the physical geography of a network. Specialized mining hardware, often custom-built application-specific integrated circuits, is expensive to buy and consumes significant power, so mining operations tend to cluster wherever electricity is cheap and cooling is manageable. This has produced large industrial mining farms rather than the hobbyist image many people still associate with the word miner.

Consider a concrete case: a small operator running two mining machines at home is contributing a tiny sliver of total network hash power, maybe a fraction of a percent. Solo mining at that scale could mean waiting years for a single block reward by pure chance. By joining a pool, that same operator instead receives small, frequent payouts reflecting their actual share of work performed, even though the pool as a whole finds blocks regularly. The underlying mining process has not changed, but the way rewards are distributed among the miners performing it has been restructured entirely around managing risk and payout variance.
